# Why each rule exists

Every rule in Fragment Architecture exists because something broke without it. This page is the receipts.

All of these happened in one repo, over four days, with two people and two different AI agents working in turns.

---

## "Every document must be listed in the index"

**What happened.** A 196-line file appeared in the docs folder containing setup instructions for an unrelated tool — nothing to do with the project. Nobody put it there deliberately. It had been generated by an agent, never read by a human, and sat there for an unknown number of days.

**Why it survived.** Nothing forced a human to look at the folder as a whole. Documents were only ever opened individually.

**The rule.** Every file under `docs/` is listed in `docs/README.md`. Unlisted means junk, and the guard finds it.

---

## "No dangling links"

**What happened.** Someone renamed a file through the GitHub web UI. Clean, ordinary housekeeping. It broke the index link, orphaned the renamed file, and skipped the session ritual — three violations from one rename.

CI caught all three within minutes. **The guard had been installed one hour earlier.**

**The rule.** Relative links between documents are checked. Renames are a normal operation, and normal operations should not be able to break the map silently.

---

## "Front doors stay thin"

**What happened.** Two AI tools were in use. Each reads a different instruction file by convention — `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`. The obvious approach is to write the rules in both.

**Why that fails.** They drift. Nobody diffs their instruction files. Two agents end up following two rulebooks, and the divergence is invisible until the behaviours contradict each other.

**The rule.** Rules live in `docs/AGENT-PROTOCOL.md` only. Front doors are three lines that point there. The guard fails if a front door stops pointing, and warns if one starts growing.

---

## "docs changed means STATE.md changed"

**What happened.** The most-skipped step in the session ritual is the last one: writing down where things now stand. It feels like overhead at the end of a session that already produced results.

But a session that produced results and left no trace **forces the next session to re-derive everything** — including decisions that were already made and are now silently contradicted.

**The rule.** In CI, if anything under `docs/` changed and `STATE.md` did not, the build fails. This is the one check that cannot run locally: it needs a comparison commit.

---

## "Verification recomputes, it does not cite"

**What happened.** A colleague brought research showing a trading strategy returning **8×**. The document was careful and its caveats were honest.

Recomputing from the raw data found the return was measured only over the events that had a payout — and events only have a payout when they win. **95% of the cost was invisible.** The real result was a loss.

Then, a week later, applying the same rule to the reviewer's *own* earlier numbers found those were wrong too — in the opposite direction. A four-day window had been mistaken for a full history, and a conclusion had been stated far more confidently than the data supported.

**The rule.** Verification is a separate document that recomputes from raw data. Applied without exception, including to yourself. It is the only rule here that has caught an error in both directions.

---

## "The guard, not the structure"

Every rule above is enforced by `scripts/docs-check.sh`, and the script runs in CI on every push.

That matters more than the folder layout. In this repo, within days, the guard caught: an unindexed file, a rename that broke the index, a skipped session ritual, and — twice — the person who wrote the guard forgetting to register his own document.

**A convention that depends on everyone remembering is a convention that decays.** The layout is the cheap part. The check is the part that makes it survive contact with a real week of work.
